overview:
Declared in Prague on 28 October 1918 as the Habsburg monarchy disintegrated, the new republic stitched together Bohemia, Moravia, Austrian Silesia, Slovakia and Carpathian Ruthenia — lands that had never been governed as a single unit. It inherited the industrial heartland of Austria-Hungary and, under Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, built the most durable parliamentary democracy in the region; by the mid-1930s it was effectively the last one left in central and eastern Europe. It was also, despite its name, a state of minorities. The 1930 census counted Germans at roughly 22 percent of the population, more numerous than Slovaks, with substantial Hungarian and Ruthenian communities as well, and the governing idea of a single "Czechoslovak" nation was resented by many Slovaks who had expected autonomy. Those fault lines were what Hitler exploited. At Munich in September 1938 Britain and France pressed Prague to surrender the German-speaking borderlands; Hungary and Poland took further territory, and in March 1939 what remained was carved into a German Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia and a nominally independent, Nazi-aligned Slovak state.

Occupation brought mass killing — the Jewish communities of Bohemia and Moravia were almost entirely destroyed — and reprisals such as the razing of Lidice after the assassination of Reinhard Heydrich in 1942. The state reassembled in 1945 minus Carpathian Ruthenia, ceded to the Soviet Union, and expelled close to three million ethnic Germans under the Beneš decrees, a demographic rupture that remains politically contested in the region today. Communists won the largest share of the vote in the 1946 elections and seized full power in February 1948. What followed was Stalinist rule with show trials and collectivisation, then a thaw that culminated in Alexander Dubček's 1968 attempt at "socialism with a human face." Warsaw Pact tanks ended the Prague Spring on 21 August 1968. The one reform that survived was federalisation into Czech and Slovak republics; everything else was undone in two decades of "normalisation," resisted by a small dissident current around the 1977 human rights manifesto Charter 77.

The regime fell fast once Moscow stopped guaranteeing it. Police violence against a student march in Prague on 17 November 1989 triggered demonstrations of half a million people, a general strike on 27 November, and the Communist Party's surrender of its constitutional monopoly the next day; the dissident playwright Václav Havel was president by the end of December. Free elections did not resolve the older question of what Slovakia was owed within the state, and after the June 1992 elections the Czech premier Václav Klaus and his Slovak counterpart Vladimír Mečiar concluded they could not agree on a federation. Parliament legislated the split without a referendum — polls at the time showed only about a third on each side actually wanted it — and Czechoslovakia ceased to exist at midnight on 31 December 1992.
significance: For seventy-four years this was the test case for almost every question modern Europe asked of itself: whether a multinational democracy could survive between Germany and Russia, whether appeasement bought peace, whether communism could be reformed from within, and finally whether a state could be dismantled without bloodshed. The answers it produced still shape political vocabulary — "Munich" as shorthand for capitulation, the Prague Spring as the limit case of Soviet tolerance, the Velvet Revolution as the template for negotiated, non-violent regime change in 1989. Its ending mattered too: the Velvet Divorce happened while Yugoslavia was tearing itself apart over comparable arguments, and the contrast made clear that the violence of a breakup is a matter of choices made by leaders rather than an inevitability of ethnic difference.
coverage: The dataset attaches no events at all to this story, so nothing here is drawn from it — the account rests on general reference works, and the map cannot currently place any of these moments. The written record for the period is unusually rich, but two areas are genuinely uncertain rather than merely thin: casualty and expulsion figures for the 1945–46 removal of the German population vary widely and are argued over by Czech and German historians, and much of what was known about the communist era before 1989 came filtered through either party organs or exile publications, with security-service archives only opened later and still generating revised accounts of who informed on whom.
